title: Monarch Ledger — Processing & Prompt Retention Q&A
summary: Monarch Ledger (financial ledger/payments) ran through Redwood's security posture focusing on how prompt/content data is handled, whether customer inputs are used for model training, encryption/KMS architecture, RBAC/SSO, and audit log retention. Redwood AE/SE addressed questions about data residency (EU/US), provided high-level assurances about no training on customer data pending written attestation, and discussed integration points for SIEM and e-discovery. Action items: send SOC2 Type II report, attestation for no-training, architecture diagram showing HSM/KMS flows, scoped pilot proposal.

transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2027-08-03 14:00 UTC
Duration: ~52 minutes
Attendees: Priya Shah (Redwood AE); Marcus Liu (Redwood SE); Jordan Keane (Monarch Ledger, CTO); Riley Park (Monarch Ledger, Head of Security); Samir Patel (Monarch Ledger, Lead Platform Engineer)

Auto-summary (auto-gen, may be imperfect): quick security deep-dive focusing on data flows, KMS, and explicit no-train on customer data.

[00:00] Priya Shah: Hey everyone, thanks for making time. Quick roll call—Priya from Redwood, Marcus our solutions engineer. Jordan, Riley, Samir — thanks for joining.
[00:12] Jordan Keane: Yep thanks, quick intro — Monarch Ledger handles settlement for small-fintechs, high-sensitivity PII/PHI? not PHI but definitely PII, and we have strict retention policies. We'll be evaluating Redwood for transaction enrichment and ledger reconciliation features.
[00:28] Riley Park: And security team is mainly focused on: does Redwood ever use our prompts to train upstream models, retention windows, KMS, RBAC and SSO integration, plus audit log fidelity for compliance reps.
[00:43] Marcus Liu: Great. We'll run through architecture and controls. High-level answer up front: Redwood does not train our hosted models on customer data by default; we can provide a written attestation and contractual language. For private/dedicated we have stronger isolation controls.
[01:05] Samir Patel: When you say 'do not train', is that policy or technical enforcement? We need a legal guarantee for auditors.
[01:14] Priya Shah: It's both — policy and we have mechanisms. For hosted customers we have a flag and account-level settings that opt-out of training; for enterprise we can enforce no-training and provide an attestation. I want to be clear though — I'll follow up with the exact legal text.
[01:32] Riley Park: Okay, we need that in writing. Also need details on retention: are prompts stored long-term for debug, or evanescent?
[01:40] Marcus Liu: Defaults vary by route — ephemeral conversational sessions have TTLs, but logs and traces are stored for operational purposes. We can scope retention per route — e.g., 7 days for ephemeral, 90 days for audit logs by default, configurable up to your requirement. For financial audits we often see requests for 7 years; we can discuss export/archival options.
[02:02] Jordan Keane: Seven years is a hard ask for us, will Redwood support that? Also need assurance that logs are tamper-evident.
[02:12] Marcus Liu: For longer retention we recommend an export to your archive (S3 with MFA delete) or connect to your SIEM. Our audit logs include append-only entries with signing and we can ship to your syslog or CloudWatch. The 'tamper-evident' piece is handled via signed log digests and retention policies — I'll attach the log schema.
[02:34] Riley Park: Can you confirm KMS architecture? HSM-backed? Customer keys?
[02:38] Priya Shah: Yes. Hosted customers get envelope encryption with customer-managed keys via KMS (we support cloud KMS providers and bring-your-own-key). For Private deployments we can integrate with on-prem HSMs / FIPS 140-2 devices. We also have an optional HSM-backed root key and rotate keys by policy.
[02:57] Samir Patel: Are model artifacts or cache data ever persisted in plaintext on the nodes? I'm worried about KV cache leaking prompt fragments.
[03:08] Marcus Liu: Good question. KV cache is in-memory by default and not persisted; if you enable warm start or checkpointing for performance we'd encrypt at rest. We also scrub prompt content in telemetry — we have a configurable scrubber to remove high-risk PII patterns before telemetry leaves the node. That scrubber uses regex heuristics and can be tuned with your DLP patterns.
[03:35] Jordan Keane: That scrubber — is it deterministic? We need reproducible behavior for audit.
[03:41] Marcus Liu: It's deterministic in terms of rule application, but it's not a full pseudonymization engine. For stronger requirements we offer on-the-fly pseudonymization where identifiable tokens are replaced with consistent surrogate IDs, stored only in your VPC if you choose private deployment.
[03:58] Riley Park: Okay. On SSO — we use Okta and expect SCIM provisioning and SAML. Can Redwood support that plus RBAC mapping?
[04:06] Priya Shah: Yes — SAML for SSO, SCIM for provisioning. Our RBAC supports pluggable roles: org_admin, team_admin, operator, auditor, read-only. We map groups from Okta to those roles, and can add custom roles for separation of duties.
[04:25] Samir Patel: Auditing — does the audit record include token-level cost attribution, who initiated request, IP, model variant? We need that for billing reconciliation and suspicious activity detection.
[04:36] Marcus Liu: Yes, the audit event includes: user_id, service_token_id, route, model_version, latency, region, input_size (token counts), and a hash of the prompt (we do not store prompt plaintext in the audit entry unless you opt in). The hash is salted and stored to allow dedup and matching without exposing content.
[04:58] Jordan Keane: Salted hash — can we provide the salt? For zero-knowledge?
[05:03] Marcus Liu: In dedicated/private we can let you manage salts or do client-side hashing. For hosted, we manage salts but we can provide HMAC-based proofs. We'll outline options.
[05:14] Riley Park: Any regulatory certifications? SOC 2 Type II? ISO 27001?
[05:19] Priya Shah: Yes, SOC 2 Type II and ISO 27001. We'll include the audit reports in the security pack. Also have penetration test summaries and our change management attestation.
[05:28] Jordan Keane: Good. What about data residency — we need EU-only processing for certain tenants.
[05:34] Marcus Liu: We can pin routes to regions; model routing supports regional isolation. For EU-only, you'd use our EU region endpoints and we can provide a Private deployment inside EU or guaranteed region routing for Dedicated nodes.
[05:48] Samir Patel: How about egress — do you ever cross-region for model fallback or training?
[05:53] Priya Shah: We have a smart routing policy but for customers with strict residency requirements we can disable cross-region fallback. For on-call fallback we can route to a secondary in-region replica but not cross legal boundaries.
[06:07] Jordan Keane: Okay. We need a written guarantee about no model training on our data. Marcus earlier said there is an account-level opt-out — is that enforced automatically or just policy?
[06:18] Marcus Liu: For hosted the opt-out flag prevents data contributing to internal training processes, and we segregate training pipelines. However, until the attestation is signed, the legal commitment isn't in place. For Dedicated / Private, data does not leave your infrastructure unless explicitly configured.
[06:33] Riley Park: We'll need explicit contract language and an attestation letter.
[06:36] Priya Shah: Understood — we'll produce that.
[06:40] Speaker 2: (mumble) can you also clarify prompt retention for customer support?
[06:44] Priya Shah: Yes, support access is audited and sessioned. Support engineers can only access redacted sessions, and require SSO-based elevation with approval workflow for live troubleshooting. All actions are logged with justification reasons.
[06:58] Riley Park: SIEM integration — we use Splunk; want syslog forwarder and alert hooks.
[07:03] Marcus Liu: Splunk via Heavy Forwarder, or direct API. We support webhook alerting and CloudWatch deliveries; we can set up a sample connector.
[07:12] Jordan Keane: On pseudonymization — you mentioned surrogates stored only in VPC. How are those keys protected?
[07:20] Marcus Liu: Surrogate mapping keys are encrypted with your KMS. If you bring your own KMS/HSM, we never see plaintext mapping. For hosted we can support a customer-managed key in the cloud KMS so that Redwood cannot decrypt without your permission.
[07:36] Samir Patel: For forensic requests, will Redwood cooperate to provide logs and redacted prompts? We sometimes need eDiscovery pulls.
[07:44] Priya Shah: Yes, we support eDiscovery exports; we can produce redacted or full exports depending on access and legal process. We recommend a live pull to your archive to manage long-term storage.
[07:56] Riley Park: How do you separate telemetry that is used for quality improvement from our data?
[08:01] Marcus Liu: Telemetry is separated by data plane tags and is sampled; production traces that contain content are scrubbed by default unless you opt-in to share more for debugging. We have an internal team that only handles de-identified samples under strict controls and with NDA.
[08:18] Jordan Keane: Are there any circumstances where Redwood would share our data with third parties?
[08:22] Priya Shah: Only as required by law or if you explicitly authorize integration with a partner. We surface subprocessors in our security docs.
[08:31] Samir Patel: Ok. We need to map controls to our audit framework — can you provide a controls matrix (SOC2 control -> Redwood control -> evidence)?
[08:39] Priya Shah: Yes, controls matrix included in security pack. We'll correlate to SOC2 sections and ISO controls.
[08:47] Speaker 1: (quiet) what about model updates — if Redwood updates a model, could that change behavior for our service and impact compliance?
[08:54] Marcus Liu: We have model version pinning and rollout policies. For critical routes you can pin a specific model version or configure canary rollouts with automatic rollback on regressions.
[09:06] Riley Park: Any chance of a rogue engineer extracting prompts from runtime?
[09:10] Marcus Liu: Strong controls — RBAC, SSO, MFA, and session gating. Access to raw prompt stores is limited to a handful of operations engineers and requires SSO approval and an auditable justification.
[09:23] Jordan Keane: Let's talk about the pilot — scoped as a dedicated pool in EU for 3 months? With retention set to 90 days default but ability to export to our archive for long-term retention. Costs TBD.
[09:34] Priya Shah: Sounds good. We'll propose a pilot that uses Dedicated capacity with EU-only nodes, KMS with customer-managed key, and optional pseudonymization. We'll include performance targets in the proposal.
[09:45] Samir Patel: For the pseudonymization, will that affect latency?
[09:49] Marcus Liu: A small delta — usually 5-10ms per request depending on complexity. We can benchmark during pilot.
[09:58] Riley Park: On legal, do you have a standard DPA that includes data handling and no-training clauses?
[10:03] Priya Shah: Yes, DPA templates include data processing terms and we can add explicit no-training annex for enterprise customers.
[10:12] Jordan Keane: Good. Anything else on encryption algorithms? We need AES-256, RSA-2048/4096 for signing?
[10:19] Marcus Liu: We support AES-256-GCM for data at rest, TLS1.3 in transit, and RSA/ECC for signing. HSMs support FIPS algorithms.
[10:29] Riley Park: What about key rotation windows?
[10:31] Priya Shah: Rotation policies are configurable. Defaults are 90 days for ephemeral keys and annual for root keys; can be tightened.
[10:39] Jordan Keane: One of our auditors asked about log retention and chain of custody. Can you sign a short attestation about how logs are stored and exported?
[10:47] Priya Shah: Yes — we'll include a chain-of-custody statement and our log export process in the security pack.
[10:54] Speaker 3: (typing audible) any mention of redaction of PII in transcripts?
[10:58] Marcus Liu: We support automatic redaction rules and can provide redaction reports. For PHI, we recommend a private deployment; for PII we have configurable regex and entity detectors.
[11:12] Riley Park: For tokenization — can you return consistent tokens for the same ID across requests? We need that for reconciliation.
[11:18] Marcus Liu: Yes, with pseudonymization turned on you get stable surrogate IDs scoped to your tenant. Keys that control mapping live in your KMS if you require it.
[11:27] Jordan Keane: Okay let's recap.
[11:29] Priya Shah: Recap: Redwood will send SOC2/ISO docs, pen test summary, controls matrix, written no-train attestation, architecture diagram showing KMS/HSM flow, and sample audit log schema. Monarch will confirm required retention windows and regulatory scopes and decide on pilot resources.
[11:47] Riley Park: We'll review and aim to get internal sign-off for pilot by 8/20.
[11:51] Priya Shah: Great. Any final questions?
[11:54] Samir Patel: One last thing — can you share a sandbox we can run a quick throughput + latency test from our EU region?
[11:59] Marcus Liu: Yes, we'll provide a dedicated sandbox endpoint and an initial benchmark config.
[12:06] Jordan Keane: Thanks everyone. The meeting notes are helpful.
[12:09] Priya Shah: Thanks all — we'll follow up with the pack.

(End of transcript — occasional mis-hears: 'K-V cash' for 'KV cache', 'H-S-M' spelled out, speaker label swap around 06:40.)
